# Moto Zero — Global Motorcycle Bible

**Research edition 1.0 · 4 November 2026 · Prepared for Marcel Kempers / Transitions Lab**

500 selected model profiles · 30 makes · 134 live Moto Zero part entries · 185 repair procedures · 274 symptoms indexed

## Read this first

This is a global catalogue and editorial mapping reference for building Moto Zero's motorcycle selector. It combines sourced model identities and regional evidence with proposed links to the existing repair library. It is **not a verified global top-500 sales ranking, an OEM parts catalogue, or 500 completed workshop manuals**.

Every model has a stable proposed ID, a description, evidence status, source links or an explicit research gap, relevant educational part links, maintenance/troubleshooting topics, and a photo-research link. 39 profiles also contain separately scoped manufacturer specification notes. Most year-specific technical specifications remain unverified; missing specifications must stay null in a production database.

**Compatibility status for every model: replacement-part fitment unverified.** The 8,371 model-to-part relationships below are editorial topic suggestions. A link does not prove that a specific SKU fits, nor that every regional version has the component. Hardware-specific links must be checked against the selected version before they appear as model-specific instructions. The reverse index uses exactly the same proposed relationships.

## Research method and evidence

### Selection

The scope is global, including petrol motorcycles, petrol scooters, underbones and selected electric motorcycles/scooters. Cars, ATVs and three-wheelers are outside this edition. Selection is editorial: everyday service relevance, regional coverage, recognisable model names, legacy repair demand and different drivetrain architectures. The 500 entries are not sorted by sales, and no worldwide installed-base total is inferred.

Manufacturer quotas were applied to a manually assembled candidate pool, with category coverage retained within each make. This is an explicit coverage budget, not a market-share estimate. Some entries are market-specific models/variants (for example Boxer X versus HD), while broader nameplates require generation children. Before launch, reconcile aliases and model codes; do not count colour or equipment packages as new model families.

### Evidence layers

| Layer | Meaning | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| Catalogue-backed | Exact name or published alias matched in VehiclesDB's motorcycle catalogue | Independent audit of the underlying register; current sales; technical specifications |
| Manufacturer-backed | A specific manufacturer source was read in this research | Every model year or other-market variant |
| Official-catalogue match | Normalised model text located in an official page | A reviewed technical sheet; the page may mention an older or related model |
| Manufacturer search evidence | Relevant manufacturer result found during targeted research | Full year/variant resolution |
| Candidate | Identity needs another source check | Publication readiness |
| Part/repair links | Editorial topics inferred from model category and the site's existing taxonomy | Exact fitment, failure frequency or verified procedure applicability |

Catalogue snapshot: VehiclesDB **2026.10.4**, retrieved during this research. Per-record IDs and source line links are retained. The upstream main branch can change; preserve the version and source IDs when importing.

| Identity evidence status | Profiles |
|---|---:|
| catalogue-backed | 364 |
| official-catalogue match—variant review needed | 58 |
| manufacturer-backed | 58 |
| manufacturer evidence—variant review needed | 20 |

The upstream registry catalogue is materially Europe-weighted. A country missing from a profile means evidence is absent in that dataset, not that the motorcycle was never sold there. Its “mass decile” mixes covered fleet stocks and registration flows and is not world sales. Country ranks are upstream observations with differing periods, not a harmonised 2026 ranking. They are included only as research leads.

### Current site, not the older files

The live [parts page](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/) contains 134 entries across 12 categories. All 134 part pages were retrieved to extract their existing repair and symptom links. This supersedes the earlier 45-part reference. The live repair and symptom indexes are linked in full below. Their content has been indexed, not clinically or mechanically certified.

A material limitation: several generic site pages include **K-Light 125-specific example specifications**. For instance, the [chain page](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/chain/) labels its chain-slack and sprocket reference as K-Light 125. Do not propagate these numbers into other motorcycle profiles.

## Market and implementation insights

1. **New sales and repair demand are different measures.** An older motorcycle can deserve a prominent profile because owners still maintain it. Record discontinued models without implying they remain on sale. Bajaj's [CT125X listing](https://www.bajajauto.com/bikes/ct) is an example of a useful legacy entry.
2. **Country coverage must shape selection.** Honda's [Brazil range](https://www.honda.com.br/motos/modelos), [Indonesia range](https://www.astra-honda.com/product) and [India range](https://www.honda2wheelersindia.com/) are different. A European catalogue alone misses important commuters and scooters.
3. **Manufacturer scale is context, not model ranking.** Honda reported 20.57 million units for the financial year ending March 2025 and approximately 40% global share under its definition ([source](https://global.honda/en/newsroom/news/2025/c250520eng.html)). This dated figure supports broad Honda coverage; it is not a current 2026 model-level ranking.
4. **Displacement in a name is not an exact specification.** Boxer 150 variants in Kenya are listed at 144.8 cc, and Himalayan 450 at 452 cc. Keep marketed name and measured displacement in separate fields.
5. **Similar names can hide different machines.** Suzuki's historic GSX-R250 and later GSX250R must not be merged by removing punctuation indiscriminately ([manufacturer archive](https://www.globalsuzuki.com/motorcycle/smgs/digital-archive/2_bike/sports_084.php)). Likewise, Rebel manual/DCT versions and different Himalayan platforms need separate configuration records.
6. **Generic components and purchasable parts are separate objects.** `brake_pads` is an educational category. An OEM brake-pad part number with a validated configuration range is a fitment record.
7. **Do not manufacture “top failures”.** No model-specific workshop-frequency dataset was obtained. All repair topics here are editorial starting points, not ranked failure claims. Later, measure anonymised workshop incidents per exposure, separating scheduled maintenance, wear, recalls and actual faults.
8. **Photographs need identity and permission.** No motorcycle photos have been downloaded or cleared for reuse. Per-model Commons links are discovery searches, not selected or licensed images. Store the depicted year/variant, creator, source, permission/licence and attribution before publishing.
9. **Electric models need an additional compatibility layer.** Vehicle model, battery revision, connector, communications, charger and controller firmware need explicit fields. A shared voltage or connector appearance is insufficient evidence of compatibility.
10. **The 134-part taxonomy is broad but not exhaustive.** Shaft-drive assemblies, final-drive belt hardware for cruisers, certain specialist front suspensions, DCT-specific components, traction-battery connector variants and some modern rider-assistance hardware need separate future entries. Do not force these into the scooter CVT belt category or invent links that the site does not have.

## Database design and publishing rules

Use a relational model even if the first implementation ships static JSON. Stable IDs let the website evolve without breaking URLs.

| Entity | Required fields |
|---|---|
| Make | make_id, display_name, aliases, parent/company relationship where verified |
| Model | model_id, make_id, display_name, category, description, identity_status |
| Configuration | configuration_id, model_id, market, model_year, generation, manufacturer_code, VIN/chassis range if supported, fuel system, cooling, gearbox, final drive, brake types |
| Specification | configuration_id, field, value, unit, source_url, source_scope, checked_date |
| Model-part topic | model_id/configuration_id, part_id, relationship_type, applicability_condition, evidence_status |
| Fitment | configuration_id, OEM/manufacturer_part_number, supplier, supersession, source, checked_date, verified_by |
| Repair applicability | configuration_id, repair_id, applicability, model-specific manual/reference, hazards, reviewer |
| Market evidence | model_id, country, period_start/end, metric, units, sales/registration/fleet basis, source, coverage |
| Image | model_id/configuration_id, asset_url, source_url, creator, licence/permission, attribution, depicted_year, review_status |

Use `null` for unknown specifications; never infer engine size from a badge. An empty fitment table is preferable to fabricated compatibility. Generic category mappings belong in `model_part_topics`, not `fitments`.

### Example record shape

```json
{
  "model_id": "mz-bajaj-boxer-150-x",
  "make": "Bajaj",
  "model": "Boxer 150 X",
  "market": "KE",
  "model_year": null,
  "description_status": "editorial",
  "specifications": [{
    "field": "displacement_cc",
    "value": 144.8,
    "source_url": "https://www.bajajauto.com/en-ke/bikes",
    "scope": "Kenya catalogue; year unspecified"
  }],
  "part_topics": [{
    "part_id": "chain",
    "relationship_type": "educational_candidate",
    "fitment_verified": false
  }],
  "fitments": [],
  "image": null
}
```

Suggested user flow: choose make → model → year/market/version → view relevant parts and maintenance topics. If the version is unresolved, show general educational links and say that exact fitment is not yet verified. Do not display a green “fits your bike” badge for these research mappings.

### Verification gates

- **Profile:** resolve the model's identity, aliases, market and photograph.
- **Specifications:** check the exact model-year manufacturer's sheet or manual and preserve units.
- **Repair links:** review hardware presence and the model-specific method, limits and service intervals.
- **Replacement parts:** verify OEM number and configuration range in a parts catalogue or authorised source.
- **Publication:** confirm rights, remove unresolved claims and record the reviewer/date.

### Brakes

#### ABS sensor and unit

**Part ID:** `abs` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/abs/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/brake.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The sensor reads the ring's teeth as the wheel turns and sends pulses to the control unit. If one wheel slows much faster than the bike, it is about to lock. The unit then briefly lowers brake pressure to that wheel and reapplies it, many times a second, so the tyre keeps grip. You feel this as fast pulsing at the lever. ABS cannot help if the tyres or pads are worn.

**Site buying checks:** Exact part number for your bike and wheel. Rings differ in tooth count and sensors differ in plug and length. Hydraulic units are model and software specific; a used unit may need coding. Avoid unbranded sensors; a wrong signal can disable ABS.

**Linked site repairs:** [Diagnose an ABS warning light Workshop job · 15 to 30 min assessment](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/abs-check/); [Pre-delivery inspection Workshop job · about 1.5 to 3 h including assembly and test ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/pre-delivery-inspection/); [Check the speed sensor Home workshop · 20 to 40 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/speed-sensor-check/); [Remove and refit the front wheel Home workshop · 20 to 40 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-remove-front/)

**Linked site symptoms:** [ABS warning light is on Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/abs-light/); [Brakes pulse or judder Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/brake-judder/); [Brake lever slowly sinks when held Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/lever-sinks/); [Speedometer or odometer does not work Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/speedo-dead/); [Brake lever or pedal feels spongy Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/spongy-brake/); [Wheel locks too easily Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/wheel-locks/)

#### Front disc brake

**Part ID:** `brake` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/brake/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/brake.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Squeezing the lever pushes a piston in the master cylinder. Brake fluid cannot be squashed, so it pushes the caliper pistons, which press the pads onto the spinning disc. Friction turns speed into heat. The caliper pistons are much bigger than the master cylinder piston, so a small hand force becomes a large clamping force. Air in the fluid, worn pads, a worn disc or sticking pistons all weaken the brake.

**Site buying checks:** Brake pads , Brake fluid , Brake disc , Brake hose , Brake caliper seal kits, Brake master cylinder kits. Bikes with linked brakes or ABS need parts for that exact system: CBS , ABS . Brake parts are where fake parts are most dangerous. Buy from a dealer or a trusted shop.

#### Brake cable and rod

**Part ID:** `brake_cable` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/brake_cable/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/chassis/F19.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The rod or cable turns the brake cam when you press the pedal or pull the lever. Return springs bring everything back. Cables stretch and rust; rods bend and their pivots wear. Too little free play makes the brake drag; too much makes the pedal travel far before braking.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model and year. Cable length, end fittings and adjuster type must match. Rods must have the same length and end shape. The wing nut, its trunnion (the small pivot block) and the return spring are often sold separately. Avoid cables with thin inner wire or soft outers.

#### Brake caliper

**Part ID:** `brake_caliper` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/brake_caliper/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/brake.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Brake fluid from the master cylinder pushes the pistons out, and they press the pads onto the disc. Rubber seals around each piston stop leaks and pull the piston back a tiny amount when you release the brake. On a sliding caliper, the body moves on greased pins so both pads press evenly. Dirt, rust and old fluid make pistons and pins stick.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model, year and front or rear. Caliper brand (often Nissin or a local maker) and the number and size of pistons. Seal kits are sized by piston diameter; measure or use the part number on the caliper. Mounting hole spacing and hose thread must match. Bikes with CBS or ABS: the caliper may have extra ports; it must be the exact part. Avoid unbranded calipers with rough casting and soft bleed screws.

#### Brake disc

**Part ID:** `brake_disc` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/brake_disc/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/brake.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/brake-disc/)

**Site explanation:** The disc turns with the wheel. When the pads clamp it, friction turns motion into heat, and the disc spreads and loses that heat to the air. Every stop wears a little metal off the disc as well as the pads. A disc gets thinner, can be scored by worn-out pads, and can warp or get uneven deposits from heat.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model, year and front or rear. Outer diameter, thickness, centre bore, bolt count and bolt circle must match. Many discs have the minimum thickness stamped on them ("MIN TH" followed by a number). Check whether your bike uses a fixed or a floating disc. Buy from a known maker; a cheap disc of soft or uneven steel wears pads fast and can crack.

#### Brake fluid

**Part ID:** `brake_fluid` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/brake_fluid/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/chassis/F19.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Fluid does not squash, so lever force reaches the caliper directly. Most brake fluids (DOT 3, DOT 4, DOT 5.1) are glycol based. They slowly soak up water from the air. Water lowers the boiling point, so after hard braking the fluid can boil, form vapour bubbles and give a soft lever. Water also rusts pistons from the inside.

**Site buying checks:** Use the grade written on the reservoir cap or in the manual, for example DOT 4. DOT 3, DOT 4 and DOT 5.1 are all glycol based and can mix, but fill with one type. DOT 5 is silicone based and must never be mixed with the others. Buy small sealed bottles. An opened bottle soaks up water; do not use one that has been open for a long time. Check the seal on the cap and the expiry or batch date. Cheap unbranded fluid may not meet the DOT standard.

#### Brake hose

**Part ID:** `brake_hose` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/brake_hose/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/chassis/F19.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The hose must hold high pressure without swelling. Rubber hoses age: they crack on the outside, swell inside and can bulge under pressure, which makes the lever soft. Hoses that rub on the fork or tyre, or get twisted when the bars turn, wear through.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model, year and position (front, rear, or which CBS line). Length and fitting angles must match so the hose does not stretch or rub at full lock and full suspension travel. Banjo size and bolt thread (K-Light 125 example: M10×1.25). Buy hoses marked with a DOT or SAE standard and the maker's name. Avoid hoses with no markings or crimps that look loose. Braided hoses are fine if made for your bike, but must have a protective cover where they touch paint.

#### Brake pads

**Part ID:** `brake_pads` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/brake_pads/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/photo/render-brake.jpg) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/brake-pads/)

**Site explanation:** When you brake, the caliper pistons press the pads onto the disc. The friction material wears away a little every stop. Most pads have a groove or notch that shows the wear limit. When the material is gone, the steel backing plate cuts into the disc and braking becomes very weak.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model, year, front or rear, and caliper brand. The backing plate shape and pin holes must match the old pad exactly. Pad makers use their own code (for example FA plus a number). Look it up for your bike, then compare shapes. Compound : organic (resin) pads are gentle and quiet but wear faster and fade under heavy use. Sintered (metal) pads bite harder and last longer but need a disc made for them. Use the type your bike came with unless the manual allows another. Fake pads may have friction material that falls off or contains no proper compound. Avoid pads sold loose without a box, with blurred printing, or far below normal price.

#### Combined braking unit (CBS)

**Part ID:** `cbs_unit` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/cbs_unit/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/chassis/F19.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** When the rider presses the rear brake, the CBS unit sends some pressure (or pull) to the front brake, often to one piston of a three-piston caliper. This helps new riders who use only the rear brake. The unit has seals and a plunger that can leak inside, and mechanical linkages can seize or go out of adjustment.

**Site buying checks:** The exact part number for your bike: CBS units are model-specific. Seal kits, plunger assemblies and pipes must be for the same unit. Mechanical scooter systems need the correct equaliser and cables.

#### Drum brake shoes

**Part ID:** `drum_brake` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/drum_brake/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/chassis/F19.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/brake-shoes/)

**Site explanation:** When you press the pedal or pull the lever, the rod or cable turns the cam. The cam spreads the shoes outward against the inside of the turning drum. Springs pull the shoes back when you release. The lining wears thinner, and as it does the brake arm has to turn further. Many backing plates have a wear pointer that shows when the shoes are worn out. Water, mud and oil in the drum make the brake weak.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model, year and front or rear. Shoe diameter and width must match the drum. Some shoes come with springs; check before ordering. Lining should be firmly bonded with no gaps. Old stock and some cheap shoes may contain asbestos; avoid unlabelled shoes. Fake shoes often have thin, crumbly lining. Buy branded shoes in a printed box.

#### Brake master cylinder

**Part ID:** `master_cylinder` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/master_cylinder/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/chassis/F19.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The lever pushes a piston with rubber cups through a bore filled with fluid. This sends pressure to the caliper. When you release the lever, a spring returns the piston and fluid flows back from the reservoir through a tiny port. Worn cups let fluid slip past the piston inside, so the lever sinks slowly. Dirt or swollen seals can block the return port and make the brake drag.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model, year, front or rear, and the bore size (often cast on the body, for example 1/2 or 12.7 mm). A wrong bore changes lever feel and travel. Rebuild kits must match the bore size and brand. Bikes with CBS: the rear or linked master cylinder is a special unit; match the part number. Reservoir cap seal (diaphragm) and lever must suit the body.

#### Rear brake

**Part ID:** `rear_brake` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/rear_brake/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/chassis/F19.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The rear brake steadies the bike and helps it slow down, especially at low speed and on loose ground. Because weight moves forward when braking, the rear wheel locks more easily than the front. On a drum brake the pedal turns a cam that spreads two shoes against the inside of the drum. On a disc brake the pedal pushes a master cylinder that clamps pads on a disc. On bikes with CBS, the pedal also applies part of the front brake.

**Site buying checks:** Check which type your bike has: drum (round hub with an arm and rod) or disc (caliper on the swingarm). Match make, model and year, and note whether the bike has CBS or ABS.

### Fuel and air

#### Air filter

**Part ID:** `air_filter` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/air_filter/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/air_filter.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/air-filter/)

**Site explanation:** An engine draws in a large volume of air. Dust in that air acts like sandpaper on the cylinder , rings and valves . The filter traps it. As the filter fills, the engine gets less air, the mixture goes rich, and power drops. A torn or badly seated filter lets dirt straight in.

**Site buying checks:** Match make, model and year. Fit and the sealing edge matter more than the material. Foam elements must be the right thickness and density; oil them with filter oil if the maker says so. Fakes and poor copies often have thin paper, glue gaps or a seal that does not fill the airbox. Hold a paper element to the light: you should see an even, dense pleat with no pinholes.

#### Carburettor

**Part ID:** `carb` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/carb/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/photos/carburettor-work.jpg) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Air rushing through a narrow throat (the venturi) lowers the pressure there, and fuel is pushed up from the float bowl through calibrated holes called jets. The float and needle valve keep the fuel in the bowl at a fixed level. The pilot jet feeds idle, the needle and needle jet feed mid throttle, and the main jet feeds full throttle. A choke or starter circuit adds extra fuel for cold starts. Old fuel leaves varnish that blocks the tiny jets, and the float needle wears and leaks.

**Site buying checks:** Match the make and code stamped on the body (for example a Keihin or Mikuni number) and the bore size in mm. Check inlet and outlet sizes, choke type (lever, cable or automatic), and the throttle cable fitting. Copy carburettors are common and cheap, but jets and float height often differ from the original. Compare jet numbers with your old one.

#### Engine sensors (TPS, MAP, temperature)

**Part ID:** `efi_sensors` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/efi_sensors/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/powertrain/F12.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The ECU sends 5 V to most sensors and reads the voltage that comes back. TPS shows how far the throttle is open; MAP shows engine load; the temperature sensors show how cold the engine and air are, so the ECU can add fuel and raise idle when cold. Faults usually come from wet or loose plugs and broken wires, less often from the sensor itself.

**Site buying checks:** Match the part number on the sensor. Sensors that look the same have different curves; a wrong one gives wrong fuelling with no code. Match the plug shape and pin count. Some TPS units must be set to a voltage or reset with a tool after fitting.

#### Fuel cap

**Part ID:** `fuel_cap` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/fuel_cap/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/fuel_tank.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The cap keeps fuel in, keeps rain and dust out and, where vented, lets air in as fuel is used. A rubber seal under the cap stops leaks when the tank is full. The lock and hinge get stiff with dirt, and the vent can block with dust or paint, which stops fuel flowing.

**Site buying checks:** Match make, model and year: bolt pattern, size and vent type (vented or sealed for a canister system). A cap may come with a new lock and key. Ask whether it can be keyed to your ignition key, or you will carry two keys. Check the new seal is soft and the vent path is open. Never block a vent to stop a leak.

#### Fuel filter

**Part ID:** `fuel_filter` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/fuel_filter/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/powertrain/F12.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Fine dirt blocks carburettor jets and sticks injector needles. The filter catches it first. As it fills, flow drops: the engine runs fine at idle but starves at full throttle or up hills. Injection systems also lose fuel pressure.

**Site buying checks:** Inline filters: match hose size and use a filter rated for petrol and, on injection, for system pressure. A cheap carburettor filter can burst on an injection line. In-tank filters: match the pump unit part number. Check the flow arrow. Poor filters have weak plastic and loose paper.

#### Fuel hose

**Part ID:** `fuel_line` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/fuel_line/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/powertrain/F12.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The hose must carry fuel without leaking, kinking or melting near the engine. Rubber slowly hardens and cracks from heat and fuel, especially with ethanol blends. Inside, it can break down and shed rubber bits that block jets.

**Site buying checks:** Match the inside diameter to the spigot. Too large leaks; too small splits. Use hose rated for petrol (marked for fuel, ideally ethanol-resistant). On injection, use hose rated for fuel injection pressure, or the maker's hose assembly with its connectors. Avoid clear plastic tubing as a fuel hose: it hardens and cracks.

#### Fuel pump

**Part ID:** `fuel_pump` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/fuel_pump/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/powertrain/F12.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** When you turn the key on, the ECU runs the pump for about three seconds to build pressure. It then runs whenever the engine turns. The pump pushes fuel through the hose to the injector at a steady pressure set by the regulator. Running the tank very low makes the pump suck air and run hot, and dirt or rust wears it and blocks its strainer.

**Site buying checks:** Match the pump unit part number or the exact make, model and year. Pump units differ in shape, plug, outlet and pressure. Some sellers offer a bare pump to fit into your old housing. It only works if flow and pressure match; buy a complete unit if unsure. Buy a new tank seal. Copies may have weak plastic, loose wires or a missing regulator.

#### Fuel level sender

**Part ID:** `fuel_sender` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/fuel_sender/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/fuel_tank.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** As the fuel level drops, the float sinks and moves a wiper along a resistor. The gauge reads the change in resistance and moves the needle or bars. Some bikes only have a low-fuel warning light, switched by a sensor at the bottom of the tank. Wear on the resistor track, a leaking float or dirt on the wiper makes the reading jump or stick.

**Site buying checks:** Match make, model and year. Senders differ in arm length, float shape and resistance range; a wrong one reads wrong all the time. Match the plug and the mounting (nut, ring or part of the pump). Buy a new rubber seal or washer with it.

**Linked site repairs:** [Test the fuel level sender Home workshop · 20 to 30 min for checks on the bike; 1 to 2 h if the sender is removed](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/fuel-sender-test/); [Remove rust from a fuel tank Workshop job · Assessment 20 min; treatment 1 to 2 days at a workshop](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tank-rust-treat/)

**Linked site symptoms:** [Fuel gauge reads wrong or does not move OK to ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/fuel-gauge-wrong/); [Fuel is leaking or dripping Stop now](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/fuel-leak/)

#### Fuel tank

**Part ID:** `fuel_tank` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/fuel_tank/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/fuel_tank.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The tank stores fuel and lets air in through a vent as fuel is used. On newer bikes vapour goes through a rollover valve to a charcoal canister instead of the open air. Steel tanks rust inside when water sits in them, and rust flakes block filters and pumps. Dents and cracks at mounts cause leaks.

**Site buying checks:** Match make, model and year: mounts, pump or tap opening, sender opening and cap ring differ. Check the inside of a used tank with a torch for rust and old sealer. Shake it to hear loose flakes. Buy new pump and sender seals with the tank.

#### Fuel tap

**Part ID:** `fuel_tap` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/fuel_tap/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/fuel_tank.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The tap lets fuel flow to the carburettor and stops it when the bike is parked. Two pickup tubes give a main supply and a lower reserve, so when the bike starts to stutter on ON, turning to RES gives a little more fuel. A strainer on the pickup and a sediment bowl catch dirt. Seals harden, strainers block, and vacuum diaphragms split.

**Site buying checks:** Match tank fixing (two bolts, plate or threaded nut), outlet position and outlet size. Match type: manual or vacuum. Fitting a manual tap where a vacuum tap was fitted means you must turn it off every time. Check the reserve tube length is similar to the old one, or reserve will start too early or too late. Buy a new tank seal or O-ring with the tap.

**Linked site repairs:** [Check the fuel tap, lines and flow Home workshop · 20 to 45 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/fuel-tap-line-check/); [Check the carburettor float and needle valve Home workshop · 30 to 60 min with the carburettor off](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/carb-float-check/); [Clear a flooded engine Rider job · 10 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/clear-flooded-engine/); [Drain old or contaminated fuel Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/drain-fuel/); [Replace the fuel filter Home workshop · 20 to 40 min for an inline filter; in-tank filters are workshop jobs](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/fuel-filter-replace/); [Remove rust from a fuel tank Workshop job · Assessment 20 min; treatment 1 to 2 days at a workshop](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tank-rust-treat/)

#### Fuel injector

**Part ID:** `injector` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/injector/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/powertrain/F12.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The ECU switches the injector on for a few thousandths of a second each cycle. A coil inside lifts a needle, and pressurised fuel sprays out as a fine mist through tiny holes. The longer it stays open, the more fuel goes in. Varnish from old fuel, dirt and water can block the holes or hold the needle slightly open.

**Site buying checks:** Match the part number on the injector body. Injectors differ in flow rate, spray pattern, resistance and length; a wrong one makes the engine run rich or lean all the time. Match the plug type and the O-ring sizes. Buy new O-rings and clips. Fakes and poor copies may have the right shape but the wrong flow. Buy from a dealer or a known injection parts maker.

**Linked site repairs:** [Check the fuel injector Workshop job · 10 min for home checks; 1 to 2 h at a workshop](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/injector-check/); [Clear a flooded engine Rider job · 10 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/clear-flooded-engine/); [Read engine fault codes (fuel injection) Home workshop · 15 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/efi-code-read/); [Check the oxygen sensor Workshop job · 10 min for home checks; 30 to 60 min at a workshop](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/o2-sensor-check/)

#### Intake manifold and rubber

**Part ID:** `intake_manifold` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/intake_manifold/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/carb.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The manifold carries the fuel and air mix into the engine and keeps out unmeasured air. The rubber also stops engine heat and vibration reaching the carburettor. Rubber hardens and cracks with heat and age. A crack lets in extra air, which makes the mixture lean, mostly at idle.

**Site buying checks:** Match make, model and year: length, angle and port size change the fit and the mixture. Check whether the injector hole and vacuum spigot match on injected bikes. Buy new O-rings and clamps. Poor rubbers can be hard from new or have flash on the sealing face.

**Linked site repairs:** [Find an intake air leak Home workshop · 20 to 45 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/intake-leak-test/); [Clean or replace the air filter Rider job · 15 to 40 min (estimate, plus drying time for foam)](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/air-filter-service/); [Adjust carburettor idle speed and mixture Home workshop · 20 to 40 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/carb-idle-adjust/); [Clean the carburettor Home workshop · 1.5 to 3 h](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/carburettor-clean/); [Check the fuel injector Workshop job · 10 min for home checks; 1 to 2 h at a workshop](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/injector-check/); [Clean the throttle body Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/throttle-body-clean/)

#### Oxygen sensor

**Part ID:** `o2_sensor` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/o2_sensor/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/exhaust_4t.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The sensor measures how much oxygen is left in the exhaust. High voltage means a rich mix (too much fuel), low voltage means lean. The ECU reads this and trims the fuel to keep the mix close to the ideal, which keeps the catalytic converter working and fuel use low. A heater inside gets it to working temperature quickly. Oil smoke, leaded fuel, silicone sealant and long rich running coat the tip and make it slow or dead.

**Site buying checks:** Match the part number, thread, number of wires (heated sensors have three or four) and plug. Wire length matters; do not cut and splice sensor wires unless the maker allows it. New sensors often come with anti-seize on the thread; do not let it touch the tip.

#### Throttle body

**Part ID:** `throttle_body` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/throttle_body/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/throttle_body.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Opening the throttle turns the butterfly and lets more air in. The ECU reads how far it is open and how much air flows, then sets the fuel. At idle the butterfly is almost shut and the idle motor lets a small, controlled amount of air past it. Oil vapour from the breather and dust leave a sticky black film that upsets the idle.

**Site buying checks:** Match the code cast or stamped on the body (K-Light 125: "30C-21") and the bore size. A body from another model can have a different sensor, idle motor or cable pulley. Check whether the price includes the throttle position sensor and idle motor. Buy new O-rings and the intake rubber if it is cracked.

### Electric drive and battery

#### 12 V auxiliary battery (electric)

**Part ID:** `aux_battery` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/aux_battery/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/battery_12v.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/battery/)

**Site explanation:** The 12 V battery powers the dashboard, lights, horn, key switch and control electronics. It also "wakes up" the system so the main contactor can close and the bike can go to ready. While the bike is on, the DC-DC converter recharges it from the traction pack. If the 12 V battery is flat, the bike can seem completely dead even with a full traction pack.

**Site buying checks:** The battery code, size and terminal position on the old battery or in the manual. Chemistry: lead-acid (AGM) and lithium 12 V batteries need different chargers. Fit the type the maker specifies. Buy fresh stock from a known brand; check the date code.

#### Battery management system

**Part ID:** `bms` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/bms/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/electrical/F26.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The BMS measures cell voltages, pack current and temperature. It stops charging when cells are full (overcharge), stops discharge when they are empty (over-discharge), and cuts power if current is too high, there is a short circuit, or the pack is too hot or cold. It balances cells so they stay at the same charge level, works out the percentage shown on the dash (state of charge) and battery health, and talks to the controller, charger and dashboard. When it cuts power, it is protecting the pack; the cause is often a weak cell, a cold pack or a charger fault.

**Site buying checks:** Not a rider part. A BMS must be programmed for the exact cell type, number of cells and pack design. A wrong or generic BMS can let cells overcharge and catch fire. Never fit a "bypass" or remove the BMS to get more power.

#### Charge port

**Part ID:** `charge_port` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/charge_port/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/charge_port.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The port carries charging current from the charger to the pack through metal pins. Many ports also have small signal pins that let the charger and BMS talk, and that stop charging if the plug is not fully in. A loose, dirty or corroded pin has higher resistance, so it gets hot under charging current. Heat then damages the plastic and makes the contact worse.

**Site buying checks:** Exact part for your bike: connector type, pin layout, current rating and wiring must match the charger. Do not fit a different connector to use another charger. Port replacement involves high-voltage wiring: buy and fit through a trained technician.

#### Charger

**Part ID:** `charger` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/charger/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/charge_port.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/ev-charger/)

**Site explanation:** The charger controls voltage and current to suit the battery chemistry and talks to the BMS on many bikes. It usually charges fast at first, then slows as the pack gets full, then stops. A fan or fins cool it. A wrong charger can push too much voltage or current into the pack and cause overheating or fire. Chargers fail from heat, dust, water, dropped units and damaged cables.

**Site buying checks:** Use the charger supplied with the bike or one the maker approves. Output voltage, current and the charge profile must match your battery's chemistry and voltage. The connector and any communication pins must match. Input must suit your mains supply. Buy from the maker or an approved dealer. Fake chargers are a major fire risk and may lack protections.

#### Main contactor and pre-charge

**Part ID:** `contactor` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/contactor/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/electrical/F25.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** When you switch on, the system first closes the pre-charge path. Current flows slowly through the resistor and charges the controller's capacitors. When their voltage is close to the battery voltage, the main contactor closes and full power is available; the bike shows ready. Without pre-charge, closing the contactor would cause a huge surge that pits the contacts and stresses the capacitors. When you switch off or there is a fault, the contactor opens to cut high voltage. Pitted or welded contacts, a burnt pre-charge resistor or a weak 12 V supply to the coil stop the bike going to ready.

**Site buying checks:** Exact part for your bike: voltage and current rating, coil voltage, mounting and connector. A contactor rated too low can weld shut. Pre-charge resistors must match the value and power rating in the maker's parts list. Not a rider or home part.

#### Motor controller

**Part ID:** `controller` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/controller/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/controller.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/ev-controller/)

**Site explanation:** The controller is the bike's power brain. It reads the throttle and turns the battery's DC power into timed three-phase current for the motor, switching large transistors on and off very fast. It also limits current to protect the battery and motor, cuts power when you brake or the side stand is down, reduces power if it or the motor gets too hot (limp mode), controls regenerative braking, and reports error codes. Inside are large capacitors that can stay charged after the bike is switched off. Heat, water and loose connectors cause most failures.

**Site buying checks:** Exact controller for your bike: battery voltage, current rating, motor type, sensor type, connectors and software. A wrong or generic controller can overheat the motor or battery. Some controllers must be programmed for the bike; buy through the maker or dealer.

#### DC-DC converter

**Part ID:** `dc_dc` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/dc_dc/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/electrical/F25.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** An electric bike has no alternator. The DC-DC converter does that job: it powers the lights, horn, dashboard and control electronics and keeps the 12 V auxiliary battery charged while the bike is on. In good designs the high-voltage side is isolated from the 12 V side inside the box. If it fails, the bike runs on the 12 V battery alone until that goes flat, and then lights, dash and the ready system stop.

**Site buying checks:** Exact part for your bike: input voltage range, output voltage and current, connectors and mounting. A generic converter may not be isolated or may not suit the pack voltage. Buy through the maker or dealer.

#### Electric motor

**Part ID:** `motor` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/motor/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/motor.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Most are brushless permanent magnet motors. Copper windings (the stator) and strong magnets (the rotor) sit close together. The controller sends current through the windings in turn, which makes a turning magnetic field that pulls the magnets round. In a direct-drive hub the windings are fixed on the axle and the magnet ring turns with the wheel. Geared hubs add a small reduction gearbox inside. With no brushes, the main wearing parts are the bearings, the gears (in geared hubs) and the cables where they leave the axle. Heat is the enemy: long climbs and overloading can overheat windings and weaken magnets.

**Site buying checks:** Exact motor for your bike: voltage, power, wheel size, axle size, cable connector, sensor type and controller compatibility. A motor not matched to the controller may judder or overheat. Hub motor bearings: the code printed on the bearing. Buy from the bike maker or approved dealer.

#### Motor position sensor

**Part ID:** `motor_sensor` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/motor_sensor/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/electrical/F24.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Each Hall sensor switches its output high or low as a magnet passes. From these signals the controller knows which winding to power next, so the motor starts smoothly and turns in the right direction. If one sensor fails or a sensor wire breaks, the controller gets the timing wrong. The motor may judder, growl, pull weakly, run only after a push, or not start, and the controller may show a sensor error.

**Site buying checks:** The exact sensor type for the motor (Hall sensor part code, or resolver model). Sensor spacing in the motor must match what the controller expects. Buy as part of a motor service kit from the maker where possible.

#### Electric throttle sensor

**Part ID:** `throttle_sensor` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/throttle_sensor/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/controller.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Most use a Hall effect sensor: a small magnet in the grip moves past a sensor chip, and the chip's output voltage changes with grip position. The three wires are a supply from the controller, a ground and the signal back. The controller turns the signal into motor current. A spring returns the grip to closed. Water, a cracked housing, a broken wire in the bars or a loose magnet give a jumpy or missing signal. A signal stuck high is dangerous because the motor can keep driving.

**Site buying checks:** Exact part for your bike. Supply voltage, signal range, connector and wire order differ between makers. A wrong throttle can give full power at rest. Check the connector shape and the number of pins; some grips include switches. Buy from the maker or dealer; cheap universal throttles often use a different signal range.

#### Traction battery pack

**Part ID:** `traction_battery` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/traction_battery/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/battery_hv.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The cells store energy and give it to the Motor controller at a voltage much higher than a 12 V battery. That voltage can give a dangerous shock. The BMS watches each cell and cuts power if something is wrong. Every charge and discharge wears the cells a little, so range slowly falls. Heat, deep discharge, charging when very cold, water and knocks speed up wear and can damage cells. A damaged lithium cell can overheat and burn without warning, and these fires are very hard to put out.

**Site buying checks:** The exact pack model and part number for your bike: voltage, capacity (Ah or kWh), connector, BMS communication and size must all match. Chemistry (for example LFP or NMC) must suit the charger and controller. Buy from the bike maker or an approved dealer. Counterfeit packs and chargers are a major fire risk. Register the pack for recall notices. Swap batteries belong to the swap network; report faults to the operator.

### Wheels and tyres

#### Wheel axle and spacers

**Part ID:** `axle` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/axle/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/wheels/W02.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The axle holds the wheel in place and lets the bearings carry it. The spacers keep the disc centred in the caliper and the sprocket in line with the chain. A bent axle makes the wheel wobble and wears bearings; a missing spacer pulls the wheel out of line and can let the brake disc rub.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model, year, front or rear. Diameter, length and thread (for example M14×1.5). Spacers must match length and inner and outer diameter exactly; take the old ones to the shop. Buy a new nut and split pin with it.

**Linked site repairs:** [Remove and refit the front wheel Home workshop · 20 to 40 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-remove-front/); [Remove and refit the rear wheel Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-remove-rear/); [Check and adjust chain slack Rider job · 20 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/chain-adjust/); [Check hub motor bearings and play Home workshop · 15 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/ev-hub-motor-check/); [Check chassis fasteners Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/fastener-check/); [Align the front wheel, forks and handlebar Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/front-end-align/); [Check wheel bearings Home workshop · 15 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-bearing-check/); [Replace wheel bearings Workshop job · assessment 20 min; replacement about 45 to 90 min per wheel](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-bearing-replace/); [Check a wheel for runout Home workshop · 20 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-runout-check/)

#### Front tyre

**Part ID:** `front_tyre` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/front_tyre/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/wheels/F20.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/tyres/)

**Site explanation:** Air pressure inside the tyre carries the load. The tread pattern clears water, and the rubber grips the road. Running the tyre under-inflated makes it flex, heat up and wear on the edges; over-inflated it wears in the centre and grips less. Rubber also ages and cracks even if the tread is good.

**Site buying checks:** Size , for example 90/90-17: 90 mm wide; sidewall height 90 % of the width; "-" means bias construction (R means radial); 17 inch rim. Load index and speed letter , a number and a letter after the size: must be at least what the manual or the original tyre shows. TL (tubeless) or TT (tube type). Match your rim. Front only or a rotation arrow: fit it the right way round. Date code : the last four digits of the DOT number are week and year (2423 = week 24 of 2023). Avoid old stock. Use the same type and tread design front and rear if you can.

#### Front wheel

**Part ID:** `front_wheel` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/front_wheel/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/front_wheel_spoked.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The wheel carries the front of the bike, steers it and takes the full force of the front brake. It must run straight and round. Potholes dent rims and bend them; loose spokes let the rim go out of true; worn bearings let the wheel rock on the axle.

**Site buying checks:** Most people buy Wheel bearings , a Front tyre , Spokes and nipples , a Tyre valve or Wheel axle and spacers . A complete wheel must match make, model and year, brake type (disc or drum), rim size and tubeless or tube type. Rim size code , for example 1.85×17: rim width in inches × diameter in inches. The tyre must suit both. Rims marked "TL" or "tubeless" can take tubeless tyres; spoked rims usually need a tube.

#### Inner tube

**Part ID:** `inner_tube` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/inner_tube/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/wheels/F20.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/tyres/)

**Site explanation:** The tube holds air pressure; the tyre gives it shape and grip. A tube loses air fast when punctured, so a flat comes on suddenly. Tubes are pinched during fitting, chafed by sharp spoke ends or a missing rim tape, and damaged if ridden flat.

**Site buying checks:** The tube size printed on it must match the tyre size, for example 2.75/3.00-17 or 90/90-17. Many tubes cover a range; check the tyre size falls in it. Valve type and length: straight or bent. Match the old one so it reaches through the rim. Never put a tube inside a tyre on a rim made for tubeless only unless the tyre maker allows it; the rim edge can chafe and overheat the tube. Heavy duty tubes resist punctures better on rough roads. Avoid thin, cheap tubes with poor seams.

**Linked site repairs:** [Repair a puncture in an inner tube Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tube-puncture-repair/); [Replace a tyre Workshop job · assessment 15 min; fitting about 30 to 60 min per wheel](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tyre-replace/); [Check and tighten spokes Home workshop · 20 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/spoke-tension/); [Inspect tyres for wear and damage Rider job · 10 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tyre-inspect/); [Check and replace a tyre valve Home workshop · 10 min to check; 30 to 60 min to replace](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/valve-check/)

**Linked site symptoms:** [Flat tyre on a wheel with an inner tube Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/puncture-tube/); [Tyre slowly loses air Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/slow-puncture/); [Air leaking from the tyre valve Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/valve-leak/); [Spokes are loose or broken Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/loose-spokes/); [Rim is dented or cracked Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/rim-damage/); [Tyre has a bulge or cut Stop now](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/tyre-bulge/); [Tyre is cracked or old Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/tyre-cracked/)

#### Rear tyre

**Part ID:** `rear_tyre` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/rear_tyre/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/wheels/F20.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/tyres/)

**Site explanation:** Air pressure carries the load; the tread clears water; the rubber grips for drive and braking. Because it drives the bike, the rear tyre usually wears faster than the front, mainly in the centre on straight roads. Overloading and low pressure make it overheat and wear fast.

**Site buying checks:** Size , for example 130/90-15: 130 mm wide; sidewall 90 % of width; "-" is bias, "R" is radial; 15 inch rim. Load index and speed letter : at least the original rating. Rear tyres often need a higher load index. TL or TT to match the rim; Rear marking and rotation arrow. Date code (DOT, last four digits = week and year). Avoid old stock. A wider tyre than standard may rub the chain or swingarm. Stay with the sizes the manual lists.

#### Rear wheel

**Part ID:** `rear_wheel` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/rear_wheel/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/rear_wheel_spoked.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The rear wheel carries most of the weight and passes the drive force to the road. It must run straight and in line with the front wheel. Chain adjusters set both chain slack and wheel alignment, so uneven adjustment pulls the wheel out of line. Bearings, spokes and rims wear and get damaged the same way as at the front.

**Site buying checks:** Usually: Wheel bearings , Rear tyre , Cush drive rubbers , Spokes and nipples , Wheel axle and spacers . A complete wheel must match make, model, year, rim size, brake type, sprocket carrier type and tube or tubeless. Rim code, for example 3.00×15: width × diameter in inches.

**Linked site repairs:** [Remove and refit the rear wheel Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-remove-rear/); [Check and adjust chain slack Rider job · 20 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/chain-adjust/); #### Spokes and nipples

**Part ID:** `spokes` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/spokes/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/front_wheel_spoked.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The spokes hold the rim round and in line with the hub. Each one is under tension; together they carry the load. If some spokes get loose, the others take more load, the rim goes out of true, and spokes start to break. Rust, potholes and overloading cause most problems.

**Site buying checks:** Make, model, year, front or rear, and left or right side: spoke length and head bend angle differ (inner and outer spokes). Spoke gauge (thickness) and thread must match the nipple. Buy complete spoke sets for a rebuild, made for your hub and rim.

**Linked site repairs:** [Check and tighten spokes Home workshop · 20 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/spoke-tension/); [Check a wheel for runout Home workshop · 20 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-runout-check/)

**Linked site symptoms:** [Spokes are loose or broken Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/loose-spokes/); [Wheel is buckled or wobbles Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/wheel-buckled/); [Handlebars shake or wobble Stop now](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/headshake/); [Flat tyre on a wheel with an inner tube Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/puncture-tube/); [Rim is dented or cracked Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/rim-damage/); [Vibration at certain speeds Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/speed-vibration/)

**Proposed model links (0):** No model-level assignment yet. Resolve specific hardware before adding this component; absence here does not mean incompatible.

#### Tyre valve

**Part ID:** `tyre_valve` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/tyre_valve/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/wheels/F20.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The core lets air in and stops it coming out. The cap keeps out dirt and water and is a second seal. Rubber snap-in stems age, crack and can be bent by the wheel spinning at speed. Dirt on the core seat makes it leak slowly.

**Site buying checks:** Tubeless rims: the stem type and rim hole size (snap-in rubber or bolt-in metal). Some bikes use angled stems for better access. Cores are a standard car and motorcycle type in most markets, but check. Buy stems from tyre shops or known brands; cheap rubber cracks fast in sun.

**Linked site repairs:** [Check and replace a tyre valve Home workshop · 10 min to check; 30 to 60 min to replace](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/valve-check/); [Repair a puncture in an inner tube Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tube-puncture-repair/); [Plug a tubeless tyre puncture Rider job · 15 to 25 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tubeless-plug/); [Inspect tyres for wear and damage Rider job · 10 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tyre-inspect/); [Check tyre pressure Rider job · 5 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tyre-pressure-check/); [Replace a tyre Workshop job · assessment 15 min; fitting about 30 to 60 min per wheel](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/tyre-replace/)

**Linked site symptoms:** [Air leaking from the tyre valve Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/valve-leak/); [Tyre slowly loses air Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/slow-puncture/); [Air leaking where the tyre meets the rim Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/bead-leak/); [Flat tyre on a wheel with an inner tube Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/puncture-tube/); [Flat tyre on a tubeless wheel Do not ride](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/puncture-tubeless/); [Tyre is cracked or old Ride with care](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/problems/tyre-cracked/)

#### Wheel bearings

**Part ID:** `wheel_bearing` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/wheel_bearing/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/wheels/W02.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/wheel-bearings/)

**Site explanation:** The balls roll between an inner and an outer ring, so the wheel turns freely on the fixed axle. Rubber seals keep grease in and water out. Pressure washing, deep water and age let water in; the grease washes out and the races rust and pit. A worn bearing feels rough and lets the wheel rock, which affects braking and steering.

**Site buying checks:** The number printed on the bearing seal, for example 6202-2RS. The four digits set the size; a 6202 is 15 mm inside, 35 mm outside and 11 mm wide. The suffix shows sealing: 2RS (or 2RS1, 2RSH) means rubber seals both sides; 2Z means metal shields. For wheels, use sealed (2RS) unless the manual says otherwise. Fakes of famous bearing brands are common. Buy from an authorised dealer, check the printing is sharp and the box is not damaged or re-sealed. A cheap unbranded bearing from a known factory is better than a fake famous name.

**Linked site repairs:** [Check wheel bearings Home workshop · 15 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-bearing-check/); [Replace wheel bearings Workshop job · assessment 20 min; replacement about 45 to 90 min per wheel](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-bearing-replace/); [Check a brake disc Home workshop · 20 to 40 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/brake-disc-check/); [Check for brake drag Home workshop · 15 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/brake-drag-check/); [Check the cush drive rubbers Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/cush-drive-check/); [Check hub motor bearings and play Home workshop · 15 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/ev-hub-motor-check/); [Diagnose a motor fault Workshop job · 30 to 60 min first assessment](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/ev-motor-diagnosis/); [Check the swingarm pivot Home workshop · 20 to 45 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/swingarm-check/); [Remove and refit the front wheel Home workshop · 20 to 40 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-remove-front/); [Remove and refit the rear wheel Home workshop · 30 to 60 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-remove-rear/); [Check a wheel for runout Home workshop · 20 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/wheel-runout-check/)

### Electrical

#### 12 V battery

**Part ID:** `battery` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/battery/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/battery_12v.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/battery/)

**Site explanation:** The battery powers the starter and, on most bikes, the ignition, lights and horn. The regulator rectifier recharges it while the engine runs. A lead-acid battery left flat grows hard sulphate on its plates and loses capacity. Heat, overcharging and deep discharge shorten its life.

**Site buying checks:** Match the code , voltage, capacity (Ah), size, terminal position and type. In a code like YTX7A-BS: Y is the maker (Yuasa), T means sealed AGM construction, X is the product family, and BS means terminals and packaging, with acid supplied in a separate pack. Other makers' batteries with the same letters after the first are made to fit the same place. Do not fit a flooded battery where a sealed one was fitted, as the K-Light manual warns. Lithium needs a compatible charging system and charger. Check the date code; an old battery that sat uncharged for months may already be weak.

**Linked site repairs:** [Test the charging system Home workshop · 20 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/charging-system-test/); [Test and charge a 12 V battery Home workshop · 15 min to test; charging takes many hours](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/battery-test-charge/); [Replace a 12 V battery Home workshop · 20 to 40 min, plus first charge](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/battery-replace/); #### Brake light switches

**Part ID:** `brake_light_switch` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/brake_light_switch/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/electrical/EL02.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** When you pull the lever or press the pedal, the switch closes and the brake light comes on. The rear switch is adjusted so the light comes on just as the brake starts to bite. Switches get dirt and water inside, springs stretch, and the lever plunger sticks.

**Site buying checks:** Match make, model and year, and type: lever plunger, pedal pull switch, or hydraulic pressure switch with the right thread. Pressure switches are part of the brake system; a leak there is a brake failure. Buy from a dealer.

#### Earth (ground) connections

**Part ID:** `earth_strap` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/earth_strap/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/wiring/WR01.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Every circuit needs a path back to the battery. On a motorcycle that path is mostly the frame and engine. If an earth is loose, rusty or painted over, current struggles to get back, so lights go dim, the starter turns slowly and electronics give strange faults. The joint can also get hot.

**Site buying checks:** Match length, wire thickness and terminal hole size. The starter earth must be as thick as the starter cable. Use tinned copper terminals and crimp them properly.

#### Indicator flasher relay

**Part ID:** `flasher` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/flasher/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/electrical/EL01.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** The flasher switches the indicator current on and off to make the bulbs blink. Older thermal flashers rely on the current of the bulbs to time the flash, so a blown bulb or a change to LED indicators makes them flash fast, slow or not at all. Electronic flashers are less fussy, and "LED" flashers work with very low loads. Heat, vibration and water kill them.

**Site buying checks:** Match pin count, pin layout and plug. A two-pin flasher is not the same as a three-pin one. Match the load type: standard bulbs or LED. If you fit LED indicators, fit an LED-rated flasher or the resistors the indicator maker supplies. Check the voltage is 12 V and the flash rate is legal where you ride.

**Linked site repairs:** [Test the indicator flasher relay Home workshop · 15 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/flasher-test/); [Fit LED indicators correctly Home workshop · 45 to 90 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/led-indicator-fit/); [Check fuses and relays Rider job · 10 to 30 min](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/repairs/fuse-relay-check/)

#### Fuses

**Part ID:** `fuse` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/fuse/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/wiring/WR01.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** If a wire rubs through and touches the frame (a short circuit), current rises very fast and the wire could melt and start a fire. The fuse melts first and cuts the circuit. A fuse does not wear out in normal use. When one blows, something caused it: find that cause before fitting a new one.

**Site buying checks:** Fit the same rating (amps) and same size and type (mini blade, standard blade, glass). The rating is printed on top. Never fit a larger fuse, a wire or foil: the wiring can burn. Blade fuses are colour coded by rating, but always read the number. Cheap fuses may blow late or not at all. Buy fuses from a known maker in sealed packs. Carry spares of each rating on the bike.

#### Handlebar switches

**Part ID:** `handlebar_switches` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/handlebar_switches/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/electrical/EL01.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Each button or lever closes or opens small contacts inside the housing. The kill switch must be closed (RUN) for the ignition to work. Contacts are small and exposed to rain, washing and dust. They corrode, get gummed with old grease, or the springs and plastic slides break. Wires can break where the loom flexes at the bar.

**Site buying checks:** Match make, model and year, and the plug and wire colours. Compare with the switch table in your manual. Check the functions match: some housings add a hazard switch, a pass switch or a light on/off switch. Check the housing fits your bar diameter and has the locating pin hole.

#### Headlight and bulb

**Part ID:** `headlight` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/headlight/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/headlight_round.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/part/headlight/)

**Site explanation:** The bulb lights the road and makes you visible. The reflector and lens shape the beam so low beam does not blind others. Halogen filaments wear and break from vibration, heat and high charging voltage. Oil from your fingers on the glass makes a hot spot that shortens life. Water inside the unit fogs and rusts the reflector.

**Site buying checks:** Match bulb type (for example H4), voltage (12 V) and wattage from your manual or the old bulb. Look for an approval mark ("E" in a circle and a number) on bulbs and lamps. Philips notes that some marked bulbs still have a poor beam because cheap makers do not keep production to the approved design; buy from brands that also supply the bike makers. Very high wattage bulbs overload the wiring and switch. LED "retrofit" bulbs in a halogen lamp can give a poor, glaring beam and may not be legal; check local rules.

#### Horn

**Part ID:** `horn` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/horn/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/illustrations/electrical/EL01.png) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Pressing the button sends 12 V to the horn. An electromagnet inside pulls a steel diaphragm, which opens contacts and releases it, many times a second, making the sound. Its low front position means it takes water, mud and stones. Contacts burn, the tone screw moves, and terminals rust. A weak battery makes it croak.

**Site buying checks:** Match voltage (12 V), mounting bracket and terminal type. Most commuter horns are 12 V disc horns. Louder horns can draw more current than the button and wiring can carry; they then need a relay. Look for an approval mark on the horn. The K-Light horn carries one.

#### Ignition switch

**Part ID:** `ignition_switch` · [Part guide](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/repair/parts/ignition_switch/) · [Existing image reference](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/assets/renders/instruments_analogue.webp) · [Existing shop destination](https://motobike-five.vercel.app/parts/)

**Site explanation:** Turning the key to ON connects battery power to the rest of the bike: ignition, injection or CDI, lights, horn and instruments. In OFF or LOCK every circuit is open. The switch has small contacts inside that carry all this current. They wear, get dirty or burn, and water and dust get in. A worn key or lock barrel makes the key stiff or loose.

**Site buying checks:** Match make, model and year: number of positions (OFF, ON, LOCK, PARK), wire colours, plug and mounting. Switches are often sold as a lock set with tank cap and seat lock, all with one key. Buying only the switch means two keys. Cheap switches can have thin contacts that heat up. A melted plug is a warning to check the whole circuit, not just the switch.
